itineraryStops.name: Busan Port pickup (cruise terminal)
itineraryStops.description:
Pickup is in the **arrival hall of whichever Busan cruise terminal your ship berths at** — the Busan International Cruise Terminal (Yeongdo) or the Busan Port International Passenger Terminal (Choryang). Neither is a default: it depends on where your ship docks, and it is confirmed at booking.

After disembarking, follow the signs to the arrival hall. Your guide is waiting there with an AtoC Korea sign and a printed itinerary card. Please be at the meeting point **by 08:50 for a 09:00 departure**.

The day runs about **8 hours**, ending back at your terminal around 17:00. The guide reconfirms your ship's all-aboard time at pickup and adjusts the running order if your sail-away is unusually early.
highlights: Direct cruise terminal pickup
Schedule follows ship arrival
Guide sign/contact confirmed before tour
**Lunch break** at a guide-recommended Busan restaurant (own expense, ₩10–15k)
**Boarding 30 min after ship clearance** (immigration buffer)
itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: Picking you up in the terminal arrival hall removes the one thing that goes wrong on a port day: finding local transport with a clock running. The 09:00 meet leaves clear time after the ship's morning disembarkation and still fits the full nine-stop route into an eight-hour day, back at the terminal by 17:00.

itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: The route's iconic anchor — the most-photographed temple in Busan, with a 650-year history and a rare Korean seaside Buddhist setting. The 09:30 arrival window lands before the major tour-bus surge (typically 11:00 onward) so the 108-stair descent and the Haesu Gwaneum viewpoint are still walkable without queuing. From the cruise terminal it is also the most efficient morning anchor — the van drives one direction (northeast along Gwangan Bridge) to the temple, then swings back across the city for the remaining seven stops without crisscrossing.

itineraryStops.description:
**Haedong Yonggungsa (해동 용궁사) — Korea's most famous seaside Buddhist temple** — perches on the rocky cliffs of Gijang-gun on Busan's northeastern coast, one of the very few major Korean temples NOT set in the mountains. Originally founded in **1376 during the Goryeo Dynasty by the great Buddhist teacher Naong Hyegeun (나옹 혜근, 1320–1376)** — a royal consultant and master who would help shape Korean Buddhism into the early Joseon era. 

Per legend, Naong was practicing asceticism at Bunhwangsa Temple in Gyeongju during a national drought; the East Sea god appeared to him in a dream and told him that building a temple on Bongrae Mountain (the original name of this seaside cliff) would restore the kingdom's prosperity. 

Naong founded the temple and named it **Bomunsa**, dedicated to Gwanseum-bosal (관세음보살, the Bodhisattva of Compassion). The temple was destroyed in the **Japanese Imjin Invasion of 1592** and lay in ruins for over 300 years until **Monk Ungang of Tongdosa Temple began reconstruction in the early 1930s**. 

The current name, **Haedong Yonggungsa (Korean Dragon Palace Temple)**, dates only to **1974** — when Head Monk Jeong-am, during a 100-day prayer (jeong-geon kido), had a vision of the Goddess of Mercy descending on the back of a dragon, emanating multicolor light. 

The temple was renamed to honor this vision. The visit follows the temple's signature processional path: through the row of **12 Sibiji-shin (Twelve Zodiac Generals)** at the entry plaza, past the **7-story 'No-Accident Pagoda'** (where drivers leave coin offerings under a stone wheel-shrine), down the famous **108 stone stairs** (representing the 108 delusions of the Buddhist mind) through a small bamboo grove, and out onto the seaside terraces and Daeungjeon main hall. 

The **Haesu Gwaneum Daebul** (Sea-Goddess of Mercy statue) on the upper cliff is the most photographed view, framing both the temple rooftops and the East Sea. 

Hours **04:30–19:20 daily, last entry 18:50, FREE admission**. **Buddha's Birthday (May)** brings Yeondunhoe lantern festival displays.

visitBasics.walking: Moderate — 108 steps through pine grove, multiple seaside terraces and stairs

itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: The route's **moral counterweight** — Busan's identity is inseparable from its role as the only Korean city the North Korean Army never captured during the war (population spiked from 880,000 to 1.4 million as refugees flooded south). Gamcheon's hillside refugee settlement and Jagalchi's 'ajumma' fish-vendor culture both trace directly to this same Korean War narrative. Visiting UNMCK before Gamcheon and Jagalchi gives cruise guests the historical context that makes the rest of the day's stops more than just photo opportunities. The 11:05 arrival also lands well inside the May–Sep evening 18:00 close (or Oct–Apr 17:00 close).

convenience.parking: On-site van lot — free for first 90 min, then ₩1,200/hr
convenience.restroom: Available at Memorial Service Hall and visitor center

itineraryStops.description:
**The UN Memorial Cemetery in Korea (재한유엔기념공원, UNMCK)** is the **only United Nations memorial cemetery anywhere in the world** — established January 18, 1951 by the UN Command during the Korean War, dedicated April 6, 1951 by US General Matthew Ridgway, and formally donated to the United Nations by the Republic of Korea in **1959** in gratitude for the UN forces who died defending South Korea. 

**22 sending nations participated in the Korean War (1950–1953)** under the UN flag — 16 nations sent combat troops + 5 sent medical aid + 1 sent observers. Initially up to **11,000 graves** were here; most fallen were repatriated post-armistice, leaving today **2,300 graves from 11 countries** (UK, US, Türkiye, Canada, Australia, Netherlands, France, Norway, South Korea, New Zealand, South Africa). 

The visit walks the cemetery's main monumental sequence: (1) the **Main Gate** (designed by Korean architect Kim Joong-up, built by Busan City in 1966 — the eight roof-supporting pillars symbolize the moment and eternity of soldiers' standing watch); (2) the **Memorial Service Hall** featuring a 12-minute documentary in English/Korean on the cemetery's history; (3) the **Symbolic Area** where the **22 sending-state flags + Korean + UN flag** fly daily; (4) the **Wall of Remembrance**, completed **2006**, with all **40,896 UN casualty names inscribed on 140 marble panels** — many veterans' relatives find their ancestors here for the first time; and (5) the **US Korean War Memorial**, dedicated **2013** with the Frank Gaylord sculpture commissioned by the American Battle Monuments Commission. 

**Hours: 09:00–18:00 (May–Sep) / 09:00–17:00 (Oct–Apr); FREE; 100% wheelchair-accessible**. Annual **'Turn Toward Busan' silent ceremony** Nov 11 11:00 AM, where the world turns symbolically toward this cemetery.

visitBasics.walking: Easy — flat grass paths and paved walkways across 14 ha of grounds; 100% wheelchair-accessible

itineraryStops.name: Lunch at a local Busan restaurant (own expense)
itineraryStops.description:
Lunch is at a coach-friendly local restaurant en route from Haeundae back across central Busan toward UN Memorial Cemetery in Nam-gu. Two typical options depending on coach routing and group preference: (1) **Dwaeji Gukbap (돼지국밥)** — Busan's signature pork-bone broth rice soup, the city's working-class comfort food since the Korean War refugee era, served with kkakdugi radish kimchi, saeujeot shrimp paste, buchu chives, and rice (~9,000-12,000 KRW per bowl); recommended in the Seomyeon or Daeyeon-dong neighborhoods, or (2) **Milmyeon (밀면)** — Busan's wheat-flour cold noodles, an adaptation of North Korean Pyongyang naengmyeon by refugees who couldn't find buckwheat in wartime Busan, served in chilled beef-broth or in spicy bibim style (~8,000-11,000 KRW). 

Both are **regional specialties unique to Busan and not commonly found in Seoul**. Lunch is at the guest's own expense; vegetarian and halal-friendly options are limited at most dwaeji-gukbap restaurants — please notify the guide at booking if dietary accommodations are needed and a separate restaurant (typically a bibimbap or hansik buffet) will be substituted. 

Total time ~60 min including parking + ordering + eating + restroom + boarding the coach.
highlights: Lunch is at your own expense — it is not included in the tour price
**Dwaeji-gukbap** (Busan pork-bone soup) or **milmyeon** (Busan cold wheat noodles) — both regional specialities
Both dishes have Korean War refugee origins unique to Busan
Typical price ₩8,000–12,000 per dish; drinks ₩3,000–6,000 if ordered
Vegetarian / halal-friendly substitution available on request at booking
itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: A flexible lunch keeps the group comfortable before the downtown and village stops.

smartNotes.photo: Dwaeji Gukbap (pork-and-rice soup, Busan's signature comfort dish from the Korean War refugee era) or Milmyeon (Busan's wheat-noodle answer to North Korean naengmyeon, originated in 1950s refugee kitchens) make the strongest local food images.
smartNotes.tip: **Vegetarian / halal / allergen requests need 24h advance notice**. Driver recommends per party preference (Korean / seafood / international); ride the recommendation or request a specific cuisine at morning pickup.

convenience.parking: Driver drops off and waits at nearest legal stand

visitBasics.admission: Pay direct, ~₩10,000–25,000 per person; lunch is NOT included in tour price

itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: Busan's identity is built on seafood the way Seoul's is built on royal Joseon palace cuisine, and Jagalchi is the single most essential expression of it. It also sits at the entrance to the Nampo-dong cluster, which is why the middle of the day pivots here: Jagalchi, BIFF Square and Gukje Market are three separate stops inside a 600 m walking radius, done on foot rather than by road.

convenience.parking: Basement lot at the main building (₩700 / 10 min); van drops off and waits in Jagalchi public lot
convenience.restroom: Available inside the main building on each floor

itineraryStops.description:
**Jagalchi Market (자갈치시장)** — **Korea's largest seafood market** and one of Busan's ten landmarks — sits on the Nampo Port waterfront in Jung-gu, a 7-minute walk from Jagalchi Station (Line 1) or Nampo Station. 

The name **'Jagalchi'** comes from **'jagal' (자갈, gravel)**, after the pebbly shoreline that once lined the area. The market's modern character was forged after the **Korean War (1950–1953)**: when many men were away fighting or had been lost in combat, **widowed and displaced women — the legendary 'Jagalchi Ajumma' (자갈치 아주머니)** — became their families' breadwinners by selling fish on wooden boxes along the pierside. 

The ajumma have been the **economic and cultural soul of Busan ever since**, embodying both the city's post-war recovery story and Korea's '**jeong (정)**' culture of long-term personal trust between vendor and customer. 

The current modern **seagull-shaped main building reopened in 2006** and houses ~400 vendors across 66,000 m² gross floor area: **1F** is the live-seafood market (octopus, snow crab, abalone, sea squirt, live hagfish, mackerel, sea cucumbers, hoe-grade flounders) where guests can **buy fresh seafood by weight then take it upstairs to a 2F restaurant for a small cooking fee** — the local way to eat at Jagalchi. 

**2F** is the sashimi-and-restaurant level. The dried-seafood section (anchovies, sea laver, kelp, dried squid) extends along the outdoor pier and is the most photogenic for travel snapshots. 

**Hours 05:00–22:00 daily; CLOSED 1st & 3rd Tuesdays of each month**. **Annual Jagalchi Cultural Tourism Festival** every October. On this small-group tour the visit is a brisk 40-min walk-through with guide commentary; guests who want to linger or eat a sashimi meal upstairs should consider our small-group product, which gives ~75 min at Jagalchi.

visitBasics.hours: Daily 05:00–22:00 (vendor hours vary; live-fish section officially 06:00–22:00)
visitBasics.walking: Moderate — ground floor flat (wet, can be slippery); stairs to 2F sashimi/restaurant level
visitBasics.admission: Free entry; pay-as-you-go for seafood and 2F cooking-fee

itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: BIFF Square is the natural connector between Jagalchi and Gukje Market — all three sit within the Nampo-dong cluster and can be walked end-to-end in under 10 minutes. Including BIFF Square as a standalone short stop (rather than passing through as a transit segment) acknowledges Busan's identity as **the host city of Asia's largest film festival** since 1996 — Korea's film industry has its public face here. The 25-minute stop fits the bus-tour pacing while giving guests time for one signature ssiat-hotteok and a walk past the most photographed director plaques. Designed-to-walk pedestrian street keeps the stop van-friendly: the van pre-positions toward the Gukje Market drop-off point while guests walk the corridor.

convenience.parking: No van parking inside BIFF Square (pedestrian street); van repositions toward Gukje Market while guests walk through
convenience.restroom: Lotte Department Store Gwangbok-ro Branch (free public restrooms) and CGV BIFF Square cinema lobby

itineraryStops.description:
**BIFF Square (비프광장, formerly PIFF Square)** is a 428-meter pedestrian corridor in Nampo-dong, Jung-gu, dedicated in **August 1996** to commemorate the launch of the **Busan International Film Festival (BIFF)** — Asia's largest film festival, first held that September. 

The square sits on what was historically **Korea's oldest cinema street**: the original **Bumin Theater opened here in 1924** and **Joongan Theater in 1927** during the Japanese colonial period, and the area has been the country's film exhibition heart ever since. 

The square's signature feature is **'Star Street'** — bronze-and-marble pavement plaques embedded with handprints, autographs, and birth years of internationally celebrated Korean directors and actors (Park Chan-wook, Bong Joon-ho, Kim Ki-duk, Im Kwon-taek, Choi Min-sik, and international guests including foreign film-festival jury members). 

At the Nampo-dong entrance stands the **PIFF Square ceremonial arch** that frames the square's most photographed angle. BIFF Square is also the birthplace of **'Ssiat Hotteok' (씨앗호떡)** — a Busan-specific variant of the Korean sweet pancake **'hotteok'** in which the doughy disc is split open after frying and stuffed with mixed seeds (sunflower, sesame, pumpkin, peanut) and brown sugar — a beloved Busan winter street food that has spread nationwide since the 2000s. 

Today the corridor is anchored by **CGV BIFF Square**, **Daeyoung Cinema**, and **Megabox** screens, with adjacent **Lotte Department Store Gwangbok-ro** branch a one-minute walk away. 

**Free, open-air, 24-hour pedestrian street**; the busiest period is the **BIFF festival itself (10 days each October)** when temporary screens, red-carpet events, and director Q&As fill the corridor. 

On this small-group tour the visit is a short walk-through (~25 min) connecting Jagalchi to Gukje Market — sufficient for the ssiat-hotteok stop and a few handprint photos.

visitBasics.hours: Pedestrian street open 24h; ssiat-hotteok carts typically 10:00–22:00
visitBasics.closed: Open year-round; busiest during BIFF festival (October)

**~600 m × 100 m grid of 1,500+ stalls** — one of Korea's largest traditional markets
**Six themed alleys**: Arirang Street (clothing), Gongguk Street (kitchenware), Wood Street (lumber), Cosmetics Street, Hardware Street, and Food Alley
Adjacent **Bupyeong Kkangtong Market** ('Tin Can Market') — Korea's first night market, popular for street food after sunset

itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: Gukje Market completes Nampo-dong's three-stop downtown cluster (Jagalchi → BIFF → Gukje) and is the day's most direct contact with **post-Korean War refugee history** — visible to guests at street level rather than told from a memorial. The connection to the morning's UN Memorial Cemetery is intentional: Gukje Market is where the refugees who survived the Korean War rebuilt Busan's economy from nothing, with goods bartered through US troop PXs and UN aid shipments. Where Jagalchi shows Korean food culture and BIFF Square shows Korean film culture, Gukje Market shows **Korean economic and survival culture**. The 30-minute stop is enough for the Arirang and Gongguk corridor walk-through plus a peek at the adjacent Bupyeong Kkangtong (Tin Can) night market.

convenience.parking: No van parking on-market (pedestrian); van picks up on Daecheong-ro at the market's north exit
convenience.restroom: Public restrooms inside Bupyeong Kkangtong Market building; Lotte Department Store Gwangbok-ro Branch nearby

itineraryStops.description:
**Gukje Market (국제시장, 'International Market')** is a sprawling traditional market in Jung-gu, Busan — one of Korea's largest and oldest post-war markets, occupying a **~600 m × 100 m grid of more than 1,500 stalls**. 

The market's origins trace to the post-Japanese-liberation period of **1945**, when displaced Korean traders began selling goods on the empty lot left by departing Japanese, and to the **Korean War (1950–1953)**, when massive waves of refugees fleeing south from North Korea expanded the market into the **'Gukje (International) Market'** name we know today — reflecting the **post-war black-market era** when goods flowed in from US troop PX exchanges, UN aid shipments, and worldwide imports unavailable through normal channels. 

After the great **Busan Station fire of 1953** destroyed the nearby downtown commercial district, displaced merchants permanently resettled at Gukje, cementing its dominance. 

The market is organized into **six themed alleys**: **Arirang Street** (clothing, accessories), **Gongguk Street** (kitchenware, household goods), **Wood Street** (lumber and furniture, the original 1950s specialty), **Cosmetics Street**, **Hardware Street**, and the **Food Alley** (street snacks and Busan local foods). 

Adjacent to Gukje is **Bupyeong Kkangtong Market (부평깡통시장, 'Tin Can Market')** — named for the canned-goods bartering culture of the 1950s and recognized as **Korea's first official night market**, lit and active until ~22:00. 

The market was the setting of the **2014 Korean film 'Ode to My Father' (국제시장)** — a Korean War family-memory blockbuster that drew **14 million ticket sales** and anchored a national reckoning with the refugee generation's sacrifices. 

Today Gukje and Bupyeong together form Busan's most lived-in shopping district — used daily by locals, not just tourists. **Hours: most shops 09:30–19:30 daily; many close on 1st & 3rd Sundays** (varies by section). 

On this small-group tour the visit is a brisk 30-min corridor walk-through, ideal for a quick taste of Busan's working-class commercial heritage before the van continues to Gamcheon Culture Village.

visitBasics.walking: Easy–moderate — flat paved alleys, can be crowded

itineraryStops.description:
**Gamcheon Culture Village (감천문화마을)** — nicknamed both **'Korea's Machu Picchu'** and **'Korea's Santorini'** — is a hillside neighborhood in Saha-gu, west Busan, whose pastel-painted houses cascade down in stepped rows over the slope. 

The settlement began in the **1920s–1930s** when the Busan administration relocated working-class residents away from the port. The village's character was set in **1955** when **~800 families (about 4,000 people) of the Taegeukdo religious community** — a uniquely Korean syncretic religion blending Buddhist, Confucian, and yin-yang elements, founded by **Jo Cheol-je** during the Japanese colonial period — settled here as Korean War refugees fleeing the North. 

The Taegeukdo philosophy of '**allowing others to prosper**' directly shaped the village's most distinctive feature: houses are intentionally tiered so that **no roof blocks the view of the house behind it**, with the entire community visible to the sky and the sea. Gamcheon remained one of Busan's poorest neighborhoods until **2009**, when the Korean Ministry of Culture launched the **'Dreaming of Machu Picchu in Busan'** public-art revitalization project, followed by the **'Miro Miro' (maze) project in 2010** — adding 22+ commissioned murals, sculptures, and art installations including the iconic **'Little Prince and Fox' bench** at the Sky Garden viewpoint. 

Gamcheon won the **2012 UN-HABITAT Asian Townscape Award** and now welcomes **~1.4 million visitors annually**. The visit follows the village's signature stamp-map walking route: from the entrance at the **Tourist Information Center**, up to **Sky Garden viewpoint** for the panoramic rainbow-roof shot, then down through the labyrinthine alleys past murals, hanbok rental shops, craft workshops, and small cafes. 

**The village is a living residential community** — quiet voices required, no drones, no flash photography into homes, and rubbish carried out. 

Hours **09:00–18:00 Mar–Oct / 09:00–17:00 Nov–Feb (info center)**; **village itself open 24h, FREE entry**.

**Songdo Cloud Trails (송도구름산책로)** is a 365-metre curved skywalk that runs out over the sea from the eastern end of Songdo Beach. Opened in **2016**, it replaced the older Songdo Skywalk with a longer, gently serpentine deck ending in a small island viewing platform, and it is **free and open around the clock**.

The beach it starts from is **Korea's first modern public beach**, opened in **1913** — an 800 m by 50 m crescent of fine sand on Busan's southwest coast in Seo-gu. Sections of the walkway have glass floor panels, so you can watch the water move directly beneath you.

itineraryStops.description:
**Yongdusan Park (용두산공원, 'Dragon Head Mountain Park')** — a **69,000 m²** civic park at the heart of Nampo-dong with **70 tree species** — is a layered historical site: it was once a **Joseon-era waegwan** (Choryang Wakan, the **Japanese trade-and-diplomacy enclave from 1678 to 1878**), then a Japanese **Ryūtōsan Shrine (17th–early 20th century)**, then a **Korean War refugee shantytown** (most destroyed by 1950s fires), and finally redeveloped as the modern park. 

The **120-meter-tall Busan Tower** (originally **opened 1973**, **rebranded 'Busan Diamond Tower' after a 2021 redevelopment**) is the park's centerpiece — its **observation deck top is modeled after the baldaquin (canopy) of Dabotap Pagoda (NT 20) at Bulguksa Temple in Gyeongju**, an explicit architectural quotation linking Busan's modern landmark to Silla heritage. 

The tower stands at **69m above sea level + 120m height = 189m total summit elevation**, offering **360° panoramas** to Busan Port, Yeongdo Bridge, Tsushima Island (clear days), and Jagalchi Market below. Other park monuments: the **bronze statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin (1545–1598)** (Busan's hometown naval hero who defeated Japanese forces in the 1592–1598 Imjin War, famously **never lost a single ship**), the **Citizens' Bell** donated by **100,000 Busan citizens** (struck **33 times on New Year's Eve and March 1 Independence Movement Day** — the 33 strikes commemorate the 33 Korean signatories of the 1919 Declaration of Independence read at Tapgol Park in Seoul; ties Busan's civic identity to national independence narrative), the **flower clock** at the entrance, and a **bronze dragon sculpture** symbolic of the mountain's name. 

Access is via a **covered escalator from Gwangbok-ro Fashion Street** (no return escalator — descend by stairs). **Park free 24h**; **Busan Diamond Tower observatory ₩12,000 adult / ₩9,000 senior 65+ or child 3–12, hours 10:00–22:00 (last admission 21:30) — observatory ticket NOT included in this tour**.

staticQuestions.question: Will the tour be full on busy cruise days?
staticQuestions.answer: The shared van seats up to 12 passengers. On peak cruise days, multiple vans may operate rather than overcrowding a single vehicle, so you may join cruise guests from different ships.

staticQuestions.question: What if my ship arrives very early — can I still join?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes. Early pickup (before 08:00) is available with a ₩10,000 per-person surcharge. This is useful for cruises with 06:00–07:00 arrivals where the standard 09:00 start would otherwise leave you waiting two hours at the terminal.

staticQuestions.question: Is lunch included?
staticQuestions.answer: No. Lunch is free time at a guide-recommended local Busan restaurant; budget ₩10,000–₩20,000 per person. Common choices are dwaeji-gukbap (Busan-style pork-and-rice soup), milmyeon (cold wheat noodles), or a bibimbap set. The guide can route to vegetarian, halal, or gluten-free kitchens with advance notice at booking.

staticQuestions.question: How is this different from a private Busan cruise tour?
staticQuestions.answer: Private cruise tours run only for your group, with a customizable itinerary and door-of-ship pickup, typically $90–$120+ per person (or $300–$500+ per group). This shared-van version runs at $68.95 per person on a fixed circuit. Choose this for budget; choose private if you want flexibility, accessibility, or to skip standard stops.

staticQuestions.question: What if Gamcheon's stairs are too much?
staticQuestions.answer: Gamcheon's main photo zones are reachable by short walk from the bus drop-off — only deeper exploration requires the steep stairs. The guide can route you through the accessible upper section of the village. If mobility is a concern, advise at booking; for full accessibility a private tour with route adjustments is a better fit.

staticQuestions.question: Can I customize the itinerary?
staticQuestions.answer: Limited — this is a fixed-route shared product. The guide can adjust timing within the route (spend longer at Gamcheon, less at Yongdusan, etc.) but cannot swap or drop stops. For full customization, a private Busan cruise tour is the right choice.

staticQuestions.question: Is the Busan Tower observatory ticket included?
staticQuestions.answer: No — the observatory is optional (₩12,000 adult, ₩9,000 youth). Yongdusan Park itself is free and gives a strong city view at ground level. Most groups skip the observatory due to the time cost vs. the time available; if you want to go up, advise the guide on arrival so they can build it into your stop time.

staticQuestions.question: Can I ride the Songdo Marine Cable Car?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes — it is the Songdo Sky Park stop, and it is your choice on the day. The cable car is not included in the tour price: you buy at the base station, ₩17,000 adult round-trip or ₩25,000 for the glass-floored Crystal cabin. If you would rather not ride, spend the stop on the free Cloud Trails skywalk and the beach promenade instead; the vehicle waits either way.

staticQuestions.question: Can we eat at Jagalchi instead of the lunch restaurant?
staticQuestions.answer: The route reaches Jagalchi at 16:00 — past lunch and before dinner — so eating there means streetfood snacks, hwe (raw sliced fish from a stall), or just browsing. If your priority is a Jagalchi seafood meal, advise at booking; the guide can move the lunch slot but the tour's pacing assumes the standard mid-day restaurant break.

staticQuestions.question: Is this a good choice for first-time visitors to Busan?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes — it covers the most distinctive Busan stops in a single balanced day, with a mix of memorial, coast, art village, viewpoint, and market. First-time visitors with one cruise port-call day are the primary audience for this product.

staticQuestions.question: How much walking is there?
staticQuestions.answer: ≈5–6 km total plus the 108 stairs at Yonggungsa (skippable), the Gamcheon hillside, and the Yongdusan stair descent. UN Cemetery, Jagalchi, BIFF Square, Gukje Market, and Songdo Beach are flat. Comfortable walking shoes with grip are essential.

staticQuestions.question: Is this suitable for children?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes, age 6 and up. Yonggungsa stairs, Gamcheon hillside, and Yongdusan stair descent are the main physical considerations. Kids tend to like the live-fish floor at Jagalchi, the ssiat-hotteok at BIFF Square, and the Cloud Trails skywalk at Songdo. Strollers are not viable at Gamcheon or Yongdusan.

staticQuestions.question: Is this OK for seniors?
staticQuestions.answer: Challenging due to Yonggungsa stairs and Gamcheon hillside. Active seniors are fine; mobility-limited travelers should consider our private cruise charter where the route can be modified to skip the steepest stops.

staticQuestions.question: What's the recommended minimum age?
staticQuestions.answer: Best fit is around age 8 and up. Children younger than that may struggle with Gamcheon's stairs and the full-day pace. If you bring younger kids, advise at booking so the guide can plan around the limit.

staticQuestions.question: What if it rains?
staticQuestions.answer: Light rain: tour runs as scheduled. Heavy rain: Yonggungsa's lower temple area becomes slippery, Gamcheon's stairs unsafe, Songdo Cloud Trails closed in storms — the guide will shorten outdoor time and extend indoor stops (Jagalchi, BIFF Square, Gukje Market). Typhoon-level weather or port closure: full refund or cruise-line rebooking arranged.

routeShapeIntro.title: How this day flows
routeShapeIntro.subtitle: A circular shore-excursion route built around Busan's port. Unlike the Incheon equivalent, Busan's main attractions are within 30 minutes of the cruise terminal — meaning more time at sights and less time on the road. The route hits the four most-photographed Busan stops (Gamcheon, Taejongdae, Jagalchi, Busan Tower) plus the city's most thoughtful Korean War heritage site (UN Cemetery), all coordinated to your ship's all-aboard time.

routeLogicSections.title: Why this route is built this way

items.label: All five Busan signatures, with a return buffer
items.detail: Many cruise day tours skip either the UN Cemetery (too sober for a beach day) or Gamcheon (too far from the port). This route includes both, plus Taejongdae, Yongdusan/Busan Tower, and Jagalchi/Nampo-dong, and still leaves a 60-minute safety buffer for the return drive. The 8-hour period is built around realistic Busan traffic, not a brochure-ideal schedule.

items.label: Built around cruise timing
items.detail: Pickup is planned to your ship's actual arrival, not a fixed start. Ships that arrive before 07:00 trigger an early-bird option (₩10,000/person surcharge) so you don't waste time at the terminal. Drop-off is timed to leave at least a 60-minute buffer before your stated all-aboard time.

items.label: Certified bilingual guide, no shopping detours
items.detail: Guides are licensed by the Korea Tourism Organization and fluent in English and Chinese. There are no ginseng shops, duty-free stops, or commissioned souvenir detours — every minute of the day is at attractions or in transit. This is rarer than it sounds for cruise group tours.

items.label: Shared-van price between coach and private tour
items.detail: Private Busan cruise excursions run $300–500+ per group. Coach tours run 40+ passengers at a low per-person price. This shared-van version sits between, with up to 12 passengers per departure — accessible for solo cruisers, couples, and small groups who don't need a private vehicle. Trade-off: fixed circuit, not customizable.

practicalAccordionItems.title: What's included
practicalAccordionItems.content: Air-conditioned shared van, certified English/Chinese-speaking guide, fuel/tolls/parking. Not included: lunch (≈₩10,000–₩20,000), optional Taejongdae Danubi Train (₩4,000 adult), optional Busan Tower observatory (₩12,000 adult), Gamcheon stamp-tour map (₩2,000), tips. UN Cemetery, Yongdusan Park, Gamcheon village, and Jagalchi Market are all free to enter. Total typical out-of-pocket: ₩20,000–₩40,000 per person.

practicalAccordionItems.title: Pickup & drop-off
practicalAccordionItems.content: Group meets at the Busan Port International Passenger Terminal arrival hall. Pickup time is planned to your ship's actual disembarkation, not a fixed start. Provide ship name, port-call date, expected disembarkation time, and all-aboard time at booking. Early pickup (before 08:00) adds ₩10,000 per person.

practicalAccordionItems.title: Sail-away timing
practicalAccordionItems.content: Drop-off at the cruise terminal at least 60 minutes before your all-aboard time. Cruise rule of thumb: be back on the ship at least 30 minutes before stated departure. The guide tracks every passenger's individual ship schedule and prioritizes return order if multiple ships sail at different times. The route is built with a 60-minute buffer for return-drive traffic.

practicalAccordionItems.title: Walking & terrain
practicalAccordionItems.content: Moderate. Gamcheon Village has steep alleys and stairs (built into a hillside) — not wheelchair-friendly, and stroller-difficult. Taejongdae's full cliff loop is 4.3 km but the optional Danubi Train (₩4,000) avoids the climb. UN Cemetery and Yongdusan are flat. Total walking: ≈3–5 km depending on Taejongdae/Gamcheon choices. Comfortable closed-toe shoes essential.

practicalAccordionItems.title: Cancellation
practicalAccordionItems.content: Free cancellation up to 24 hours before pickup. Same-day cancellations and no-shows non-refundable. If your ship's port call is cancelled by the cruise line, full refund with cancellation documentation.

practicalAccordionItems.title: Children & accessibility
practicalAccordionItems.content: Children age 8 and up are welcome and the route works well for them — Taejongdae's Danubi Train is a kid favorite, and Jagalchi's live fish are reliably interesting. Strollers are not viable at Gamcheon (stairs); other stops accept them. Wheelchair users should consider a private cruise tour with route adjustments — Gamcheon and Taejongdae's cliff trail are the bottlenecks.

staticQuestions.question: Will the tour be full on busy cruise days?
staticQuestions.answer: The shared van seats up to 12 passengers. On peak cruise days, multiple vans may operate rather than overcrowding a single vehicle, so you may join cruise guests from different ships.

staticQuestions.question: What if my ship arrives very early — can I still join?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes. Early pickup (before 08:00) is available with a ₩10,000 per-person surcharge. This is useful for cruises with 06:00–07:00 arrivals where the standard 08:30 start would otherwise leave you waiting two hours at the terminal.

staticQuestions.question: Is lunch included?
staticQuestions.answer: No. Lunch is free time at a guide-recommended local Busan restaurant; budget ₩10,000–₩20,000 per person. Common choices are dwaeji-gukbap (Busan-style pork-and-rice soup), milmyeon (cold wheat noodles), or a bibimbap set. The guide can route to vegetarian, halal, or gluten-free kitchens with advance notice at booking.

staticQuestions.question: How is this different from a private Busan cruise tour?
staticQuestions.answer: Private cruise tours run only for your group, with a customizable itinerary and door-of-ship pickup, typically $90–$120+ per person (or $300–$500+ per group). This shared-van version runs at $58.50 per person on a fixed circuit. Choose this for budget; choose private if you want flexibility, accessibility, or to skip standard stops.

staticQuestions.question: What if Gamcheon's stairs are too much?
staticQuestions.answer: Gamcheon's main photo zones are reachable by short walk from the bus drop-off — only deeper exploration requires the steep stairs. The guide can route you through the accessible upper section of the village. If mobility is a concern, advise at booking; for full accessibility a private tour with route adjustments is a better fit.

staticQuestions.question: Can I customize the itinerary?
staticQuestions.answer: Limited — this is a fixed-route shared product. The guide can adjust timing within the route (spend longer at Gamcheon, less at Yongdusan, etc.) but cannot swap or drop stops. For full customization, a private Busan cruise tour is the right choice.

staticQuestions.question: Is the Busan Tower observatory ticket included?
staticQuestions.answer: No — the observatory is optional (₩12,000 adult, ₩9,000 youth). Yongdusan Park itself is free and gives a strong city view at ground level. Most groups skip the observatory due to the time cost vs. the time available; if you want to go up, advise the guide on arrival so they can build it into your stop time.

staticQuestions.question: Should we take the Danubi Train at Taejongdae?
staticQuestions.answer: If you have any concern about the 4.3 km cliff loop, yes — the Danubi Train (₩4,000 adult) covers the loop in ≈30 minutes with stops at the lighthouse and the cliff viewpoint, and it solves the climb at the start. Active walkers can do the trail in 60–75 minutes. The 75-minute stop time accommodates either choice.

staticQuestions.question: Can we eat at Jagalchi instead of the lunch restaurant?
staticQuestions.answer: The route reaches Jagalchi at 16:00 — past lunch and before dinner — so eating there means streetfood snacks, hwe (raw sliced fish from a stall), or just browsing. If your priority is a Jagalchi seafood meal, advise at booking; the guide can move the lunch slot but the tour's pacing assumes the standard mid-day restaurant break.

staticQuestions.question: Is this a good choice for first-time visitors to Busan?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes — it covers the most distinctive Busan stops in a single balanced day, with a mix of memorial, coast, art village, viewpoint, and market. First-time visitors with one cruise port-call day are the primary audience for this product.

staticQuestions.question: How much walking is there?
staticQuestions.answer: ≈3–5 km depending on choices. Gamcheon's hillside alleys and Taejongdae's cliff trail are the active sections; UN Cemetery and Yongdusan are flat. The Danubi Train at Taejongdae is an option to skip the climb. Comfortable closed-toe shoes are essential.

staticQuestions.question: Is this suitable for families with children?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes for school-age children (≈8+) who can manage Gamcheon's stairs. Kids tend to respond best to the Danubi Train at Taejongdae and the live-fish floor at Jagalchi. The UN Cemetery is short and quiet.

staticQuestions.question: Can older adults join comfortably?
staticQuestions.answer: Active seniors are fine; the Danubi Train solves Taejongdae and the Gamcheon upper section is mostly walkable. Travelers with significant mobility limitations should consider a private cruise tour instead — Gamcheon's hillside is the bottleneck.

staticQuestions.question: What's the recommended minimum age?
staticQuestions.answer: Best fit is around age 8 and up. Children younger than that may struggle with Gamcheon's stairs and the full-day pace. If you bring younger kids, advise at booking so the guide can plan around the limit.

staticQuestions.question: What if there's heavy rain or a typhoon?
staticQuestions.answer: Light rain: tour operates as planned. Heavy rain: Taejongdae's cliff trail may close, while the Danubi Train may still operate. Gamcheon remains open but can be more limited for photos. If a typhoon warning is issued, rebooking or full refund is offered. If the cruise line cancels your port call, full refund applies with cancellation proof.
